projectBackground.name: Orion SaaS Reforecast
projectBackground.timeline: Reforecast due before the quarterly board pack
projectBackground.context: Orion's first-half results missed plan. The CFO wants an honest reforecast with the drivers explained, not a plug number.

manager.name: Marta Keller
manager.note: Don't give me a number without the driver behind it. If revenue is down, tell me whether it's price, volume or mix — and what you'd assume for the second half.

assignment.title: Explain the miss and rebuild the second-half forecast
assignment.brief: Calculate margin and variances, model three scenarios in Excel, and write a short CFO memo with a recommended case.

documents.name: Orion H1 Management Accounts
documents.note: Revenue $4.8M annualised run-rate base; cost of goods sold $1.92M for the same period.

documents.name: Budget vs Actual — Units and Price
documents.note: Budget 10,000 units at $50; actual 9,000 units at $52.

documents.name: Scenario Assumptions Sheet
documents.note: Base revenue $2,000,000 with downside, base and upside growth rates to apply.

tasks.title: Gross Margin
tasks.prompt: Orion revenue is $4,800,000 and cost of goods sold is $1,920,000. What is the gross margin percentage?
tasks.reasoning: Gross margin is gross profit divided by revenue; the $2.88M gross profit over $4.8M revenue gives 60%.
tasks.tip: State margin as a percentage of revenue, never of cost.
tasks.mistake: Dividing gross profit by cost of goods sold gives mark-up (150%), which is a different measure.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Volume Variance
tasks.prompt: Budget was 10,000 units at $50. Actual was 9,000 units at $52. What is the sales volume variance in dollars (negative = adverse)?
tasks.reasoning: Volume variance values the unit shortfall at budget price: 1,000 fewer units x $50 = $50,000 adverse. The favourable $18,000 price variance only partly offsets it.
tasks.tip: Always split a revenue variance into price and volume before explaining it.
tasks.mistake: Reporting only the net -$32,000 hides that volume is the real problem and price is masking it.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Choosing a Forecast Approach
tasks.prompt: H1 actuals missed plan because customer sign-ups slowed. Which reforecast approach is most defensible?
options: Rebuild the second-half forecast from drivers (sign-ups, price, churn) using actuals to date, and show the assumptions
Multiply the original budget by H1 actual/budget ratio and call it done
Keep the original budget unchanged to protect the board's confidence
Add a flat 10% to H2 to recover the shortfall
tasks.reasoning: A driver-based reforecast uses what actuals revealed and exposes assumptions to challenge; scaling or hoping hides the cause.
tasks.tip: Forecast from drivers, not from totals.
tasks.mistake: Simply scaling the budget or forcing recovery assumes the cause of the miss disappears by itself.
tasks.recommendation: Label every assumption with its source and owner.

tasks.title: Assumptions to Flag
tasks.prompt: Select every assumption that should be explicitly documented in the reforecast.
options: Sales hiring plan and ramp time
Price increase timing and customer response
tasks.reasoning: Churn, pricing and sales capacity are material drivers that stakeholders can challenge. Preferences and irrelevant factors are not assumptions.
tasks.tip: If an assumption moves revenue materially, write it down.
tasks.mistake: Leaving key drivers implicit makes a forecast impossible to review or defend.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: Scenario Model (Excel)
tasks.prompt: Base revenue is $2,000,000. Project next-year revenue under three growth rates in column D (Projected Revenue = Base x (1 + Growth)). Download the template, complete it, and upload.
tasks.reasoning: A scenario table lets the CFO see the range of outcomes; the formula should reference the inputs so it can be flexed.
tasks.tip: Use formulas referencing input cells, not typed results.
tasks.mistake: Hard-coded results break the moment an assumption changes.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

tasks.title: CFO Memo
tasks.prompt: Write a 3-5 sentence memo to the CFO explaining the miss and recommending which scenario to plan on.
tasks.modelAnswer: Orion missed plan mainly on volume: 9,000 units against 10,000 budgeted cost $50,000, partly offset by a $18,000 favourable price variance, for a net adverse $32,000. The cause is slower sign-ups, not pricing. I recommend planning on the base case (+5% growth, $2.10M) with the downside ($1.94M) as the funding floor, and revisiting the sales ramp assumption monthly. If sign-ups recover faster than churn, the upside is credible but should not be committed in the board plan.
tasks.reasoning: A strong memo names the driver, quantifies it, recommends one case and states what would change the view.
tasks.tip: Lead with the conclusion, then the driver, then the ask.
tasks.mistake: A memo that lists numbers without a recommendation leaves the CFO to do the analyst's job.
tasks.recommendation: Write down your reasoning and the evidence behind it so a reviewer can verify your conclusion quickly.

caseStudy.title: Case Study: The Forecast Nobody Updated
caseStudy.background: A planning team kept a twelve-month forecast built in January even as sign-ups slowed. By Q3 the company missed its cash target by 14% and had to freeze hiring.
caseStudy.budget: Cash shortfall required an emergency credit line
caseStudy.challenges: The forecast still assumed January growth rates and was only compared to actuals at quarter-end.
caseStudy.constraints: No one owned the assumptions, so no one noticed they were stale.
questions: Why did a static annual forecast mislead the business?
What cadence would have caught the slowdown earlier?
Who should own each driver assumption?
caseStudy.solution: Quantis moved the client to a monthly rolling forecast with named owners for each driver and a variance trigger at 5%.
caseStudy.lessonsLearned: A forecast is only as good as the freshness of its drivers; schedule the review, name the owners and set triggers.
